power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Learning-disabled children and young people experience systemic barriers to their inclusion in research, and researcher expertise and experience can either act as one of those barriers or as a facilitator.
Researcher accounts of conducting research with learning-disabled children and young people can provide useful insights into practices that facilitate inclusion, yet such accounts are scarce.

This study presents a secondary analysis of ethnographic data collected by four researchers during a study exploring the communication preferences of learning-disabled students in a special school setting in the North of England.
It focuses on the researchers' reflections on their own experiences of data collection, as captured in their fieldnotes.

Four themes were developed using thematic analysis: (1) Moving beyond a "one-size-fits-all" approach; (2) The importance of relationships; (3) Researching as an outsider/insider; (4) Why it matters who does the research.

Findings highlight the positive, yet sometimes challenging, experiences of working with learning-disabled students in a special school setting, and contribute to the knowledge base on supporting inclusive practices for qualitative research with learning-disabled participants.

The article discusses actionable recommendations for how researchers can navigate the challenges they may encounter during data collection and considers the role of secondary analysis as a reflexive tool.

While many groups are underrepresented in research, people with learning disabilities 1 (known as intellectual disabilities in some contexts) face especially persistent barriers to inclusion (Doody, 2018; McClimens & Allmark, 2011; Porter & Lacey, 2004).
text.formatted: While many groups are underrepresented in research, people with learning disabilities 1 (known as intellectual disabilities in some contexts) face especially persistent barriers to inclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Doody, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">McClimens & Allmark, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Porter & Lacey, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Learning-disabled (LD) people can present with a complex range of physical, intellectual, and communication needs (e.g., they may be nonspeaking and/or have limited ability to access literacy (McClimens & Allmark, 2011).
text.formatted: Learning-disabled (LD) people can present with a complex range of physical, intellectual, and communication needs (e.g., they may be nonspeaking and/or have limited ability to access literacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(McClimens & Allmark, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This means that LD people are often unable to access research participation because studies are not designed with their needs in mind, and this situation is even more challenging for LD children and young people (CYP) than it is for LD adults.

Combined, this often results in LD CYP being excluded from research, or researchers using proxy reports from parents/carers, or key stakeholders rather than including LD voices (Smith et al., 2025; Yoon, 2023).
text.formatted: Combined, this often results in LD CYP being excluded from research, or researchers using proxy reports from parents/carers, or key stakeholders rather than including LD voices <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Smith et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Yoon, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This exclusion of LD CYP and overreliance on proxy reports are problematic for a number of legal and moral reasons.

Article 12 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC, 1989) explicitly declares that children have the right to express their views freely in all matters affecting them, and Article 7 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD, 2006) emphasises the importance of enacting this right with disabled children.
text.formatted: Article 12 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child <ref type="bibr">(UNCRC, 1989)</ref> explicitly declares that children have the right to express their views freely in all matters affecting them, and Article 7 of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities <ref type="bibr">(UNCRPD, 2006)</ref> emphasises the importance of enacting this right with disabled children.

text.text: Alongside this, there is a strong societal and academic push towards inclusive, participatory, and rights-based research with LD CYP; however, the systematic exclusion of LD people from research continues to deny this group the benefits that research can provide, including more effective support and amplified voices in society (Bottomley et al., 2024; Doody, 2018; Fields et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Alongside this, there is a strong societal and academic push towards inclusive, participatory, and rights-based research with LD CYP; however, the systematic exclusion of LD people from research continues to deny this group the benefits that research can provide, including more effective support and amplified voices in society <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bottomley et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Doody, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fields et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If research is not grounded in the lived experiences of LD people, it cannot meaningfully inform the services, policies, and practices that affect them.
Therefore, it is necessary to develop an understanding of, and guidance on, how to conduct research effectively with LD CYP to facilitate their meaningful participation.

The current study examined researchers' experiences whilst conducting qualitative research with LD CYP to contribute to the development of knowledge about practices that effectively facilitate participation in qualitative research for learning-disabled people.
There are several key reasons for the underrepresentation of learning-disabled people in research.
Firstly, due to the range and complexity of additional needs, there is a perception that conducting research with LD individuals is more difficult (Benstead et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Firstly, due to the range and complexity of additional needs, there is a perception that conducting research with LD individuals is more difficult <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Benstead et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In some cases, LD CYP may have additional behavioural challenges, which may be difficult for researchers to navigate (Mikulak et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In some cases, LD CYP may have additional behavioural challenges, which may be difficult for researchers to navigate <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Mikulak et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Others may have communication or comprehension differences, or use 1 For the purposes of this study, the term 'learning-disabled' refers to individuals with conditions that impact their ability to process information and live independently throughout their lives (Fields et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Others may have communication or comprehension differences, or use 1 For the purposes of this study, the term 'learning-disabled' refers to individuals with conditions that impact their ability to process information and live independently throughout their lives <ref type="bibr">(Fields et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Augmented and Alternative Communication (AAC), which may be unfamiliar to researchers.

There has historically been a lack of tools to facilitate communication with LD participants, meaning existing tools need to be carefully and collaboratively adapted to avoid confusing terms, complex grammar, and other barriers to understanding (Nicolaidis et al., 2020).
text.formatted: There has historically been a lack of tools to facilitate communication with LD participants, meaning existing tools need to be carefully and collaboratively adapted to avoid confusing terms, complex grammar, and other barriers to understanding <ref type="bibr">(Nicolaidis et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, research has identified a lack of awareness of which tools are available and how to use them effectively (Fields et al., 2025; Mikulak et al., 2024).
text.formatted: More recently, research has identified a lack of awareness of which tools are available and how to use them effectively <ref type="bibr">(Fields et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Mikulak et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This is especially true for LD CYP with higher support needs, and for individuals who do not communicate through speech, meaning these individuals may be left out of research (Doody, 2018).
text.formatted: This is especially true for LD CYP with higher support needs, and for individuals who do not communicate through speech, meaning these individuals may be left out of research <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Doody, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This presents issues for bias in research sampling and outputs that can reinforce existing inequalities (Shariq et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This presents issues for bias in research sampling and outputs that can reinforce existing inequalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Shariq et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: As a consequence of the challenges outlined above, research with LD CYP can be more timeintensive than with other populations in relation to, for example, the time required for researchers and participants to develop a relationship and get to know each other (including participants' specific needs and preferences), explain information thoroughly, and ensure that participants understand what is needed from them (Fields et al., 2025).
text.formatted: As a consequence of the challenges outlined above, research with LD CYP can be more timeintensive than with other populations in relation to, for example, the time required for researchers and participants to develop a relationship and get to know each other (including participants' specific needs and preferences), explain information thoroughly, and ensure that participants understand what is needed from them <ref type="bibr">(Fields et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Previous studies overwhelmingly highlight the need to cultivate relationships with learning-disabled participants, their caregivers, teachers, and other significant people to bring a successful research project to fruition, and this can be a lengthy and delicate process (D'Sa et al., 2024; Leishman et al., 2023).

text.text: In addition, navigating ethical approval and informed consent can be daunting when designing and carrying out research with LD CYP, often resulting in the need for research processes to be adapted and tailored to meet the individual needs of participants, meaning the level of methodological and ethical flexibility required can be difficult to achieve whilst meeting traditional research standards and expectations (Benstead et al., 2024; Runswick-Cole et al., 2024).

text.text: The issue of how to establish informed consent is a point of continuous conversation in the world of research with learning-disabled participants (e.g., Bottomley et al., 2024; Porter & Lacey, 2004), as this requires a reframing of the standard research approach from one-off consent forms to encompassing concepts such as continuous consent and recognising different forms of communicating assent (McNeilly et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The issue of how to establish informed consent is a point of continuous conversation in the world of research with learning-disabled participants (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bottomley et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Porter & Lacey, 2004)</ref>, as this requires a reframing of the standard research approach from one-off consent forms to encompassing concepts such as continuous consent and recognising different forms of communicating assent <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(McNeilly et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Good practice guidelines highlight the need to take time to fully explain to LD participants what participation in the research project entails, using accessible language or alternative resources, and to remind participants that they can withdraw at any time while the research is ongoing (Bottomley et al., 2024).

text.text: All of this can take more time and differentiation than working with and obtaining consent from non-LD individuals, and may be met with 'pushback' from academic institutions.

Indeed, Leishman et al. (2023) highlighted the inability to proceed with their project using simple, easy-read consent forms due to the imposition of university standard documentation, which ballooned the length and complexity of their documents, making them more difficult to understand and access, and going against the LD co-researchers' wishes.

(2023)</ref> highlighted the inability to proceed with their project using simple, easy-read consent forms due to the imposition of university standard documentation, which ballooned the length and complexity of their documents, making them more difficult to understand and access, and going against the LD co-researchers' wishes.

text.text: Each of these factors can pose daunting challenges for researchers unfamiliar with methods for addressing them, whilst working within the constraints of institutional requirements, yet little is known about how researchers experience and navigate such challenges whilst in the field.
This is further complicated when working with LD CYP within their educational setting.
In the United Kingdom and many countries around the world, LD CYP with more complex needs are often educated in special educational settings.

Special schools are designed to meet the specialist medical, social or welfare needs of the children and young people they support, and in England, only children with an Education and Health Care Plan (EHCP) are entitled to attend specialist provision.

This means that all children attending specialist settings have some kind of recognised additional learning need, including learning disabilities, and staff-to-student ratios are often much higher than in mainstream settings.
These setting-specific differences have several implications for researchers.

Firstly, consent from a gatekeeper, usually a head of school or a member of senior leadership, must be obtained before access to the school can be granted, which creates potential access challenges before the project has begun (Fecke et al., 2022; Williams, 2020).

text.text: Furthermore, as all children in special schools have additional and potentially more complex needs, researchers must navigate associated challenges, including medical needs, communication differences, and behavioural challenges, not only for the LD CYP they are working with but also for other CYP in the setting.
These all come with safeguarding implications.
Special schools settings are also less predictable working environments than mainstream settings.

To accommodate for their students range of needs, pedagogical approaches are necessarily flexible and responsive, and account for not only learning differences, but the management of volatile or unpredictable behaviour which is more common in these settings.
For researchers unfamiliar with special school settings and safeguarding, or, most importantly, working with LD CYP, navigating these differences may be particularly daunting.

Accounts of researchers' experiences that highlight the challenges and practicalities of conducting research in these settings are imperative for designing and conducting more inclusive and ethical research; however, their accounts are often missing from the literature. Greenstein (2014) provides an important autoethnographic example of integrating researcher reflection into research findings, documenting a single researcher's experiences in a special needs unit within a mainstream school.

text.text: This study highlighted systemic issues such as navigating institutional ethics procedures, institutional gatekeeping, and the prevalent belief that people with learning disabilities are unable to provide informed consent.

Researchers described how, when collaborating with organisations, they had to navigate barriers such as workload pressures, high staff turnover, and the need to reduce the burden on participants and caregivers.

These challenges were often rooted in negative attitudes towards the value and feasibility of research with this population, even from funders and professionals, emphasising how the academic research system's reliance on standardisation often fails to accommodate diverse needs and real-world circumstances, impacting inclusive research with LD participants.

While these accounts establish that qualitative work in special education introduces distinct reflexive and institutional challenges, they primarily examine single-observer dynamics or macro-level administrative barriers.

text.text: This paper extends current knowledge by using an independent secondary analysis of multi-researcher fieldnotes to examine individual and collective team reflexivity and fieldwork practices.
Specifically, this paper asks: • What are the experiences of researchers conducting research with learning-disabled participants in a special school setting?
• What barriers and opportunities for research with learning-disabled participants do researchers highlight whilst conducting research in a special school setting with learningdisabled participants?
This study used qualitative secondary data analysis to re-examine an existing set of ethnographic fieldnotes.
The analysis was carried out by an independent researcher who was not involved in primary data collection.

A reflexive interpretivist stance was adopted, acknowledging that the fieldnotes were qualitative representations shaped by the primary researchers' experiences in the field and subsequently interpreted through the first author's analytical lens (Willig, 2013).
text.formatted: A reflexive interpretivist stance was adopted, acknowledging that the fieldnotes were qualitative representations shaped by the primary researchers' experiences in the field and subsequently interpreted through the first author's analytical lens <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Willig, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Alongside re-analysing the dataset, we propose this analytical framework as a novel, multi-perspective reflexive tool for qualitative research.

Using an independent researcher provides a layer of objectivity, allowing for the exploration of any assumptions or normalised classroom dynamics that researchers in the field may unconsciously overlook, and facilitating the identification of areas of good practice.
The dataset comprised secondary fieldnotes originally recorded by four researchers during an ethnographic study exploring children's communication choices.
Fieldnotes were compiled over seven weeks of visiting two classes in a special school in the North of England between November and December 2024.
The full final textual data sample was 197,776 words.
All final field notes were anonymised by the primary research team ahead of this secondary data analysis.
This study examined ethnographic fieldnotes from four participants.
Participants were members of the same research team at the University of York, UK.
All participants were female and ranged in levels of research experience and seniority.

text.text: To ensure that analytical distance was maintained, and that the analysis worked as a reflexive tool, the first author, who was not involved in the primary data collection, led the process.
Familiarisation was established by reading and re-reading the fieldnotes before conducting initial coding in NVivo 15 (Lumivero, 2025).

text.text: The first author then engaged in peer debriefing by sharing their initial analysis with the co-authors who gathered the primary data.
This process integrated their field insights to clarify any contextual nuances, challenge potential analytical blind spots, and refine code groupings.
Following this, the first author revisited the codes and clustered them into candidate themes, which represented overarching patterns across the dataset.
Themes were then reviewed against the dataset to ensure their suitability, refined where needed, and assigned conceptual theme names.
The entire author team critically reviewed and agreed upon the final thematic structure.
The study for which the data were originally collected received ethical approval from the University of York, Department of Education].
The original ethical approval included approval for the data to be used anonymously in secondary analysis, in line with Open Science Guidelines.
This was made clear to participants when they agreed to take part in the primary data collection.
As a result, no further ethical approval was sought for this secondary analysis.
The first author of the current study was not involved in the initial data collection and had no prior association with the study setting or primary participants.
However, all authors had prior experience working with learning-disabled children and young people in educational contexts, which may have impacted the interpretations of the data.
All authors were colleagues in the same research lab at the University of York, so it is possible that close association may also have introduced some bias into the analysis of experiences.
However, this close association also meant it was possible to fact-check and minimise the potential for misunderstandings on the part of the first author during the secondary analysis.
Regular meetings were held by the team to challenge individual assumptions, explore alternative interpretations of the text, and ensure the final themes were grounded in the data.

Four themes were developed from the data: (1) moving beyond a "one-size fits all" approach; (2) the importance of relationship building; (3) researching as an outsider/insider; (4) the role of researcher characteristics and practices.

A key challenge evident throughout the dataset was the researchers' experiences of navigating the complex individual needs of the students, who presented with a wide array of cognitive, behavioural, and social characteristics.
These differences affected how researchers interacted with CYP throughout the study and emphasised the need for a bespoke approach to research which respected the individuals' needs and preferences.

Although the researchers received some prior information on each student's communication profile, they were usually learning and familiarising themselves with these as they went along: '[Student] strikes me as processing very slowly but having very good non-verbal social skills.' (P1).
However, occasionally they could not interpret what the student meant and had to adapt accordingly.
Researchers described how drawing on multimodal communication strategies, such as sign language or Augmented and Alternative Communication (AAC) devices, could help overcome communication challenges.

These strategies were often individual to each student, and often involved more than one form of communication, highlighting the complexities of interacting with LD CYP and making it very clear that a 'one-size-fits-all' approach is inappropriate and likely to be ineffective with these CYP in this setting.

This is evidenced by a researcher's experience of observing how a teaching assistant navigated a multimodal communication interaction with a student: notice [student] gives her AAC to [teaching assistant], and she begins signing/gesturing.
[Teaching Assistant] asks -"do you want to show me something?"
and [student] starts pointing at her AAC and points for [teaching assistant] to change the page that her AAC is on.
[Teaching assistant] moves between the pages -now [teaching assistant] and [student] are both stood up looking together.
[Student] points to the picture of the toilet and looks at [teaching assistants] face -[Teaching Assistant] asks do you want the loo?
And [student] nods.
The research team also had to navigate fluctuations in the behaviour of some young people.
On rare occasions, the researchers documented examples of transgressive behaviours on the part of the students, and very rarely there were examples of aggressive incidents.

The following incident highlights the importance of being aware of potential triggers, but also that even with awareness and preparation, behaviours can be sudden and unpredictable, and may be an unpleasant experience for researchers:
Student] leans out of her beanbag chair towards me and grabs my hair close to my scalp and is pulling it very hard.
She does this with two hands, and [Teaching Assistant] helps me get free -it hurts a lot and she asks if I'm ok -I say I am.
I was slightly surprised by the reaction of [Student], and not sure what it was linked to -perhaps I was sitting too close, perhaps because I wouldn't try the beef jerky.
While I'm thinking this and regrouping, [Teaching Assistant] suggests it's likely because [Other Staff Member] went out of the room, which will probably have upset her.

(P3) Working ethically with diverse individuals A range of experiences was evident in the assent and consent process, and researchers reflected that what worked for some young people was not appropriate for others, highlighting the need to adapt research to be bespoke to individuals from the very beginning of the research process.
Researchers were aware of and consistently sought to obtain students' assent to participate in the project.

After presenting an initial explanatory video and receiving feedback at the start of data collection, they attempted to check in with each student about their understanding of what they were taking part in and whether they were happy to participate.
There was a range of responses from students regarding the process of obtaining initial and ongoing consent/assent.

Mostly, students expressed their assent to take part in the immediate activities the researchers were doing and were happy for them to take notes about them: 'I tell her that we're writing about how people communicate and ask if that's ok.
She says "yes" and looks very bored by my explanation and walks off.' (P2).
Others were clear in stating that they did not want to take part: 'She is polite and smiles sweetly and just quietly says "no thank you."' (P1).

However, researcher experiences reflected that while the students may have been happy to take part in the immediate activities, they may not have understood the broader meaning and purpose of their involvement in the research project.
Likewise, some students opted out, but later opted back in, or chose to take part in some tasks but not others.

The researchers appeared to understand that they must revisit points with students to check not only the participant's understanding of the assent process, but that researchers own understanding of how students were interpreting the assent information provided to them.
The quote below highlights how doing so identified challenges with the wording in one of the assent questions:
Working through these, I ask her each time she says yes or no to one of the questions and permissions why.
I explain it's not because I'm changing her mind but because it's helpful for me to know why people like some things and don't like other things.
For example, she said no to videos, but yes to photos.

I asked her why this was important for her, and she says "Because I don't like to share" -this was for the question 'are you happy for us to share the videos with other people' -and she said yes for photos […] "Because I like posing.
There were also a smaller number of examples in which the researcher was rejected or rebuffed by the student when attempting to engage with them.

This drawing of boundaries represented some of the most explicit gestures of autonomy and (lack of) assent by the students, and the researchers needed to show tact and respect in these situations, demonstrating that knowing when to back off is an important skill in the context of research with learning-disabled participants: [Student] was at the head of the table with his talker […] I could see the last words used were: "Still in sonic song."
I asked him if he liked Sonic, and he looked at me and moved his talker.
I felt a bit guilty, like I was reading his thoughts, despite trying to start [a] conversation with him about something I thought he might be interested in.

Theme 2: The importance of relationship building
Researchers noted that relationship-building was vital to overcoming challenges and enhancing data collection.

Their experiences showed that communication and behavioural barriers could be alleviated by taking time to get to know the student, becoming familiar with their needs and preferences, and establishing a strong relationship.

Relationships with school staff were also described as important, as staff helped facilitate the research in the school setting, and their cooperation and support were often essential in adapting research practices to be appropriate for individual participants.

One key facilitator experienced across the four researchers was that familiarity was essential There were frequent examples of researchers building relationships by getting directly involved with activities such as playing physical games, doing crafts, music lessons, puzzles, and relaxing or playing together during breaks.
Researchers frequently expressed genuine affection for the students and desire to get to know them better, using existing knowledge of students' likes and dislikes to further develop relationships:
During this time, [Student] grabs my arm to get my attention.
She gives me the bells, and I assume she wants me to shake them for her.
I hold them up to her ear (as I've been told before that she really likes loud noises) and begin to shake them.
She smiles.

(P2) Likewise, students appeared to develop strong bonds with the researchers over time, showing preferences for spending time with them and sometimes confiding their feelings or worries, experiences which were seen as essential to successful research: Yesterday lunchtime in school, [Student] saw me from the other playground with the small class.
She gestured me over, and asked why I couldn't be with her class then.
I told her I would the next day -Friday -and she was pleased.
(P3) However, researchers occasionally experience relationship building as challenging.
Researchers sometimes perceived instances where students became too fixated on the researchers' presence or absence, which could be as disruptive to the rest of the class: "[Name]!
[Name] is reading book!
[Name]!
[Name] don't forget to write in book!
[Name] is reading and make sentence!".

I said I will write down some of the things and show [student] after tryday so everyone could see, as I was aware he was focusing more on me and my writing more than the tryday session, and I didn't want to derail the class or distract students.
Furthermore, relationships with staff were seen as crucial to successful data collection and were often cultivated by spending time in the classroom before class began or during lunch breaks.

Building relationships gave rise to ad hoc and casual interactions, and these more spontaneous interactions were seen as key parts of the research process, despite the additional time needed to 'be around' outside of specific sessions with students: "These moments for quick opportunistic chats about friendship feel like a good and low-pressure way of data collection."

Researchers were clear and consistent in their view that successful data collection could not adopt a 'one-size fits all approach', and time spent engaging informally and building up positive and familiar relationships with students and staff was essential in facilitating this.

This theme captures contrast: the researcher in the school setting is an outside observer, yet, to varying extents, becomes involved in the day-to-day activities and social dynamics of the school and classroom.
Researchers often expressed feeling out of place at the school, including worries about being intrusive or disruptive and a heightened awareness of their status as interlopers.
These experiences were often prompted by moments when a lack of familiarity with the setting left them unsure what was going on or why.
However, these were often countered by feelings of inclusion and camaraderie for staff throughout the research process.
The extent to which researchers became integrated was sometimes reflected in their descriptions of the classroom layout and their positioning within it.
Researchers sometimes chose to position themselves on the outside of the group in an observer role, and sometimes as part of the group in an active participant role.
There were benefits to the active participant role, as opportunities to play and interact directly with the students were valuable for relationship-building and data collection.
Researchers often expressed that they were happy to help and pleased to be able to contribute positively to the classroom: 'As I go out of the door [Teacher] thanks me for helping.
She hasn't said this before and I'm glad that she feels I have done something useful.' (P1).

There were many instances, likewise, where the researchers expressed empathy and camaraderie for the staff, observing that there are many complexities to working in the setting that the staff need to navigate while being overworked and, in many cases, underpaid: 'It is very clear that the teams have to adapt to constant change and to be incredibly agile to make the environment safe and meet the needs of the students.' (P1).

However, it seemed that becoming more actively involved could make role boundaries more malleable, as researchers were sometimes asked or expected to help or look after the students, particularly when they were acting hands-on with the students and activities.
These instances were sometimes experienced as stressful by the researchers:
Being told to keep people safe whilst observing feels quite stressful.
(P2) I had to leave [Student 1] and run after [Student 2].
For a while, then, I ended up responsible for both students.
(P4) On one occasion, a researcher and a member of staff came into direct conflict when the staff member asked them to perform duties the researcher felt were inappropriate and outside their remit.

As part of this, the researcher was asked to share what had been recorded about some students in their observation notes; this put the researcher in the difficult position of deciding whether to disclose any of that information.
Deciding not to disclose meant setting boundaries with the staff member, and it was difficult to do so while maintaining a good relationship to ensure the research project's success.

The tensions in the dynamic between the insider/outsider position of the researcher and the full insider position of the staff member were evident in this exchange: I'm quite taken aback […] I have the feeling that [Staff Member] perhaps took that tone with me because of feeling threatened in some way by the research, and that she was trying to take me down a peg.
This may have been related to uncertainty about the extent to which staff understood the purpose of the research and the researcher's role.

Researchers sometimes expressed concerns that their presence might seem threatening or intimidating to staff, or that staff may be changing their behaviour because they were aware of being observed: 'I think me asking questions is making her nervous and unconfident but she does seem happy to talk.' (P1).
Actively participating in classroom activities occasionally resulted in students blurring boundaries, sometimes mistaking the researcher for another classroom staff member.

Researchers reflected that this appeared to be partly related to systemic factors, such as understaffing and the continuous coming-and-going of additional supply staff: 'I guess [the students] are used to a lot of supply workers, and even though my behaviour is odd (making notes etc.)
I do have the appropriate lanyard and fob.' (P1).
This further highlights the need for clear information and ongoing monitoring of assent, as discussed in Theme 1.

Researchers continuously navigated the tension between being outsiders and insiders, balancing the benefits of rapport and meaningful contribution against the stressors of blurred boundaries and conflicting responsibilities within the school environment.

Researchers reflected that the ability to be flexible and responsive to the changing demands of students and the school environment was imperative, accepting that sometimes, students would not be up to chatting or doing activities that they might be more able to do at another time: I wondered if there was something not quite right with [Student] today as usually she is caring and considerate of other classmates and eager to chat.

Indeed, structured data collection activities did not always go as planned, sometimes due to constraints in the setting or due to students interpreting the task in an unexpected way.

The researchers needed to make decisions in the moment about how much control to exert over the activities and whether to redirect a student's focus, balancing the need to allow students to authentically express themselves with the need to collect data relevant to the research aims.

This was sometimes overcome by drawing on staff members' support, in the moment: '[Teacher] did a fab job of helping us facilitate conversations and starting the task off with the group, though the task ended up being slightly different to what we had planned.' (P4).
On this, the researchers reflected on integrating the good practices and useful strategies modelled by staff to adapt their own data collection methods.

For some, this was during data collection to better meet an individual student's needs: 'She suggested changing some of the language in their forms, e.g. instead of "share" to change that to "show", which was helpful to think about and sounds more accurate and more specific to the meaning.' (P3).

For others, it was a wider reflection on adapting future methods to be more inclusive: I notice that posting works really well and wonder if we could include a resource in our library that involves asking participants to make a picture-based choice and post their choice in a post-box.
It might suit some people.
It was clear that research in this setting requires researchers to be comfortable with some level of physical touch from students.
Some of the researchers were comfortable with greater levels of touch (e.g., hugging, hands touching the face), or unexpected touch, while others found similar levels of touch uncomfortable.

Levels of prior experience working with LD CYP appeared to play a role, with those who had spent more time in similar settings consistently expressing greater awareness of and sensitivity to boundaries and safeguarding, but being aware of the need for navigating physical touch, given that some students used this as a form of communication, and that personal space may be encroached upon:
As we get into the room [student] heads straight for me and [teacher] says 'watch her, she's a bit grabby' (she's known to pull hair sometimes).
She comes over and says "fish".

We spent The above highlights how a researcher's experiences of the setting may shape their approach to research, and that they must be comfortable adapting on the spot to overcome data-collection challenges, ensuring that their work is inclusive and ethical.
This includes the need for patience, time, and openness to changing their broader practices.

This study was a secondary analysis of ethnographic data collected by four researchers within a special school setting, analysed by an independent fifth researcher who had not been involved in the primary data collection.
The findings offer a nuanced exploration of the ethical, relational, and practical complexities that arise when conducting research alongside learning-disabled children and young people (LD CYP).
This study also demonstrates how secondary data analysis of team fieldnotes can act as a reflexive tool in qualitative research.

Researchers in this study routinely had to navigate the boundary between gathering rich qualitative data and respecting participant autonomy, building relationships with students and staff, and ensuring that patience, flexibility, and empathy were woven throughout the research process.
Researchers had varied experiences which echo and extend those reported in existing literature on research with LD CYP.
Although researchers encountered distinct challenges, strategies were often developed to overcome them, resulting in predominantly positive overall experiences.
Throughout the research process, feelings of inclusion and camaraderie were identified, showing that integrating into a special school setting can foster a deeply collaborative research environment.
Researchers were welcomed into the school setting by staff and students and made to feel part of the broader school community.
The findings support the adoption of pluralistic and adaptive qualitative methodologies when working with LD CYP and suggest that there is no singular 'right way' to do this kind of research.

While previous research with LD individuals has primarily focused on adapting research tools (Cluleyhttps://paperpile.com/c/3AXQtqFN/lTvR+vIqA 2017; Nicolaidis et al., 2020) , our findings show that methodological success is dependent on researcher flexibility and responsiveness.

In these instances, adaptability was a key facilitator, supporting Fields et al. (2025)'s findings.

text.text: Importantly, our analysis extends prior literature by demonstrating that researcher flexibility and adaptability extend to modes of communication, not just the ability to adapt research methods.

Researcher competence in multimodal communication, such as interpreting physical gestures, AAC, and sign language, must be paired with a flexible, responsive approach to work with LD CYP and problem-solve when communication breaks down.

A key contribution of the current study is highlighting how relational dynamics extend beyond participant rapport, showing that researchers must have the ability and willingness to develop and maintain good relationships, not only with the LD CYP, but with the staff that support them.
As discussed by Fields et al. (2025), familiarisation is a key and essential component of successful research.

text.text: However, existing accounts often treat staff primarily as gatekeepers for initial access (Williams, 2020).

text.text: In contrast, our findings show that relationships not only supported access to the data collection site but also actively shaped the researchers' overall experiences.

Interpersonal relationships with staff fostered inclusion and camaraderie within the team; however, they also introduced complex role blurring, such as informal requests to supervise students or share observation notes.

This tension highlights the interface between academic research standards and the established cultural norms of special school environments, demonstrating that fieldwork experiences are strongly impacted by school climate.

These findings suggest that researchers' experiences will differ across special school settings, and that having a well-prepared, reflexive research team equipped to navigate relational discomfort will be key to ensuring a successful research project.
Furthermore, navigating consent and assent, although complex, proved to be a positive and constructive experience, but one that researchers could not treat as static.

Rather than seeing consent as an initial barrierhttps://paperpile.com/c/3AXQtqFN/NHa9+EBhw as highlighted in previous literature (Leishman et al., 2023; Mulhall et al., 2021) , our findings confirm that consent functions as an ongoing, relational process (McNeilly et al., 2020).

text.text: Navigating this required researchers to remain privy to changes in participant behaviours or expressions of disengagement.

Although this added complexity to the process, it ultimately appeared to empower LD CYP by respecting their agency and choices, reinforcing a research ethos grounded in trust and dignity rather than compliance.
Our findings suggest that with thoughtful and skilled researchers, the consent process can and should be managed in a way that is accessible to LD CYP.

To facilitate this in future work, Institutional Review Boards and ethics committees must accommodate flexible, process-oriented consent frameworks that prioritise participant non-verbal assent over rigid written forms, and researchers must acknowledge that their experience of navigating consent may be different to what they are used to.
Beyond using multiple methodologies and communication modalities, the application of established qualitative principles was central to navigating these flexible methodologies.
Continuous researcher reflexivity served as both an analytical lens and an ethical safeguard (Olmos-Vega et al., 2022).

text.text: Reflexivity during the initial writing of fieldnotes allowed researchers to interrogate their own positionality, acknowledge emotional reactions to classroom events, and deliberate on power imbalances (Day, 2012).

text.text: Throughout, this experience was regarded as a helpful part of the research.

Establishing structured space for team debriefing and individual reflexivity is therefore critical for managing the emotional labour of ethnographic work in special school settings, and ensuring high standards of research integrity are maintained.

Taking this a step further, having an independent researcher review and interrogate the notes, in conversation with the researcher who made them, can add a useful additional layer of reflexivity and understanding.

Participant heterogeneity, communication, and behavioural differences were the most common challenges researchers encountered during this project (e.g., Benstead et al., 2024; Bottomley et al., 2024).

text.text: Our findings suggest that using methods that 'lean in' to what may be thought of as 'difficulties' in working with this population, such as allocating longer amounts of time for data collection and collecting data in natural settings, can not only make research more robust to unpredictability but also enhance the data collected and improve the research experience for everyone.
Using open-ended ethnographic techniques ensures data collection remains inclusive and ethically sound with this population.
Furthermore, researchers entering these settings must have access to training on managing boundaries and sensory communication beforehand to safeguard both participants and themselves.
The findings here have implications for future qualitative research with LD CYP, and the wider LD community.

It is clear that there is room to develop more specific guidance on working with learning-disabled participants, for example, on responding to behaviours such as touch, aggression, and intensive interactions (Mikulak et al., 2024).

text.text: While staff who work regularly with LD people may have routines and procedures in place, researchers entering special school settings may lack the experience or knowledge to navigate situations as they arise.
To address this need, we suggest the following recommendations based on the current studies' findings:
Table 2: Recommendations for researchers in special education settings

Understanding when a CYP has withdrawn their consent/assent • Work with staff to map how participants show refusal or disengagement and establish how young people express yes and no (e.g., shutting of eyes, turning away, specific gestures).
• Respect CYP choice to disengage, and document this in fieldnotes as a valid and autonomous mode of withdrawal • Take materials to facilitate withdrawal (e.g., stop signs, or yes and no cards).
Explicitly explain these to CYP in a way they understand.
See figure 1 for example.
Navigating staff relationships and maintaining the role of a researcher • Co-design clear boundaries regarding researcher responsibilities with the school prior to data collection beginning.
• Explain to staff, both in information sheets and verbally, what your role is and what you can and cannot help with.

• Explicitly detail how researchers will handle requests for classroom assistance; develop scripts for researchers to support declining supervisory requests where needed Managing physical contact or behavioural challenges • Work with staff to identify participants' triggers, sensory likes and dislikes, and touch preferences.
Discuss and disclose researcher preferences as well.
• Decide as a team how these instances will be recorded in notes, keeping participant dignity in mind at all times.

text.text: A key strength of this paper is its examination of researchers' first-hand experiences conducting qualitative research in a special school setting.

Few papers have focused on researcher experiences as the primary topic of a research paper, particularly when the research was carried out by a team, yet understanding these experiences are key to developing ethical and inclusive research.
A further strength is that the first author was not involved in the primary data collection, which brings a fresh perspective and a lack of expectations about what might come up during the analysis.

At the same time, members of the original research team were available to review the coding and proposed themes and to offer insights into the situations, which enriched the analysis and interpretation process.
However, secondary data analysis relies on the depth and detail of the original fieldnotes, meaning unrecorded contextual nuances cannot be directly probed.
Furthermore, the analysis is based on the experiences of a small group of researchers from a single institution within a single special school setting.

As special schools vary widely in the types of students they support, their school culture, and their leadership style, the experiences documented here may differ across mainstream inclusive settings and alternative educational provisions.

Future research should represent a wider range of settings or compare different settings to provide a broader overview of how researchers experience conducting research with learning-disabled participants in schools.
Further investigation into how engaging with longitudinal qualitative research impacts researcher-participant power dynamics would also provide valuable insights for the field.
This study examined the experiences of researchers conducting ethnographic research with LD participants in a special school setting.
Thematic analysis explored their experiences navigating the research process, the barriers and facilitators they encountered, and the strategies they developed as a result of these experiences.

By using an independent researcher to conduct the secondary analysis, the paper also demonstrated how secondary fieldnote analysis can be used as a multiperspective reflexive tool for qualitative research.

The findings extend existing research by examining the complexity of working not only with LD CYP, but also within a special school setting across team members, highlighting the importance of the characteristics and practices of the researchers, including the application of reflexivity.
It also demonstrated that consent can be successfully navigated if treated as a dynamic, relational process.
Finally, our study highlights the importance of multimodal researcher communication and structured team reflexivity.

The paper calls for researchers to move beyond generic calls for patience and flexibility, and offers actionable recommendations to support ethical and inclusive research with learning disabled children and young people in a special school setting.

Although conducting qualitative research in special school settings presents distinct relational and ethical challenges, our findings demonstrate that with appropriate reflexive frameworks, research with LD CYP is not only viable but also an enjoyable and enriching experience for those involved, and one that can amplify LD voices in a meaningful way, and in accordance with the rights of LD CYP.

highlight, transparent accounts of research processes are often missing from the literature despite being an important means of understanding what motivates researchers who work in this area and how they address the challenges they face in the field.

Crucially, existing accounts have not examined how different researchers negotiate role boundaries, continuous non-verbal consent, physical touch, and classroom expectations in real time, nor how collective fieldnotes can be analysed as secondary data, to explore individual and collective researcher reflexivity.

Hearing the experiences of other researchers could also potentially demystify the process of conducting research with LD CYP, making it more accessible and/or less intimidating for researchers who want to become involved in research with this population but lack confidence to take the first step.

Moving beyond a "one-size fits all" approach: Making research bespoke for learningdisabled studentsThis theme captures researchers' views on the challenges of conducting ethical and effective research in this setting, how those challenges affected their experience as researchers, and what they found helpful.
Challenges at the individual and group levels related to communication, understanding, and unexpected behaviours were identified.
The development of positive and respectful relationships, and mindful reflection on whether they had authentic consent to continue the research process were identified as key facilitators.
Researcher experiences navigating these individual differences all fed into a clear need for research that is adaptable and bespoke to individual participants.
As a result of learning communication preferences 'on the go', researchers reported experiencing twoway, mutual communication challenges.
Researchers were often unable to understand what a student was trying to communicate on a first attempt.

Depending on the young person researchers were working with, researchers usually managed to figure it out after a few attempts, sometimes with assistance from a staff member familiar with the student: He was saying something to me verbally and using signs at the same time and it took me a little time to figure out that he was saying 'garlic bread'.
I ask if he is talking about Peter Kay, the comedian and he says yes and laughs.
[…] He was patient waiting for me to figure out words that I was stuck on, like last time and if I struggled to understand what he said, he was ok with me asking him to show me (in signs).
(P2) in overcoming communication challenges and developing accessible and inclusive research.

Growing familiarity helped, as understanding what the students' unique needs were, as well as their interests and preoccupations, helped the researcher to 'read between the lines' and figure out what the student wanted in the event of a communication breakdown: 'My interpretation is that he is upset because he thinks there's a suggestion that he was in the wrong place and following rules and doing things right is really important to him.' (P1).

Why it matters who does the research: The role of researcher characteristics and skill setIt was clear throughout the data that conducting research with LD CYP in a special education setting required specific characteristics and responses from researchers.
Patience, empathy, and flexibility appeared to be key traits required of the researchers, which they frequently demonstrated in their fieldnotes.

She gets really close to my face and watches me.
(P2) Finally, and importantly, the researchers' application of reflexivity and self-reflection was essential to responsible data collection.
Researchers appeared to use self-reflection/reflexivity for several purposes.

Firstly, they used it to assess and monitor the impact of their own biases on the data collection process, which could change the interpretation of observations: It occurs to me that some of what I wrote about the [Activity] session I observed last week was quite negative -around a lack of focus, guidance and support for learning -but it is clear that it matters a lot to [Student], and is very worthwhile for him.
(P1) In this way, reflexivity was also used to assess what the experiences they observed meant to those involved, adding an additional dimension to the notes beyond merely documenting what happened.

The researchers frequently considered what the situations that arose meant for their own work, and what could be meaningfully drawn from their experiences to inform the research going forward:[Students] both remind me of the importance of pitching data collection tools in chronologically age-appropriate ways, even when the young person's cognitive development might be out of sync.
It is important to keep an eye on the nuance as the same person might be interested in sex and relationships but also in Peppa Pig.
This presents a challenge that needs to be taken seriously.

(P1) Not only do we need to allow time for children and young people to process the questions we have asked and formulate their responses, but researchers may need to accept that they may need processing time and not to give up on trying to understand what a young person has said so easily.
